artists.biography:
Jem Godfrey began in music as a songwriter for many pop and mainstream groups. In fact, he’s written four number one singles in the UK for groups such as Atomic Kitten and Shayne Ward. In 2004, he began the group FROST* in England and ventured into the realm of progressive rock. For his debut album, called “Milliontown”, Jem enlisted guitarist John Mitchell (Arena, Kino), bassist John Jowitt (IQ, Jadis), and drummer Andy Edwards (IQ). The album itself is a mixture of neo progressive rock, progressive metal undertones, some symphonic leanings, and some more mainstream ideals. “Milliontown” was released on July 18th 2006 in the USA and July 24th in the UK. FROST* is a band to look out for in the future and they seem to have a long, fruitful future ahead of them.

A second album titled “Experiments in Mass Appeal” was released in November 2008. Declan Burke from (Darwin’s Radio) has been added to the lineup for additional guitar and to take up lead vocals.

perplexity.description:
Falling Satellites is the third studio album by British neo-prog band Frost, released on May 27, 2016, through InsideOut Music. The album marks a significant return for the group after an eight-year hiatus, following 2008’s Experiments in Mass Appeal. Musically, Falling Satellites blends elements of progressive rock, electronic textures, and pop sensibilities, showcasing the band’s signature fusion of lush keyboards, intricate arrangements, and melodic hooks. Led by Jem Godfrey, the album features a dynamic lineup including John Mitchell on guitar, Nathan King on bass, and Craig Blundell on drums, with guest appearances from Joe Satriani and Tori Beumont. The sound is both expansive and accessible, balancing atmospheric passages with energetic, rhythm-driven tracks.

In terms of its place in Frost’s discography, Falling Satellites stands out as a creative high point, praised for its ambitious songwriting and eclectic style. Critics highlighted its depth and variety, with many considering it the band’s strongest release to date. The album received positive reviews for its well-crafted compositions, standout tracks like “Signs” and “Closer To The Sun,” and its ability to blend progressive complexity with memorable melodies. Commercially, it re-established Frost as a vital force in the modern neo-prog scene, earning acclaim from outlets such as The Prog Report and Man of Much Metal, and solidifying its reputation as a standout release in the band’s catalog.
